lead: Hawaii's water damage comes from heavy trade-wind rain, tropical storms and constant humidity. DryFlare helps owners on Oahu, Maui, Kauai and the Big Island get homes dry.
risk: flash floods from heavy rain, tropical storms and hurricanes, and humidity that feeds mold
why: Hawaii's rain falls hard and fast on steep ground. In April 2018, Kauai set a U.S. record of nearly 50 inches of rain in 24 hours, flooding Hanalei and parts of Oahu's east side. Windward sides of every island get far more rain than leeward sides. Streams can rise in minutes and send water and mud into homes.

Hurricanes and tropical storms are rarer than on the mainland coast, but they do hit. Iniki struck Kauai in 1992, and FEMA declared new disasters for Hurricanes Lala and Lowell in 2026. Many older homes are single-wall plantation style with jalousie windows, which let wind-driven rain in. High humidity means wet walls grow mold quickly. Owners with mainland homes in California will find drying here takes more dehumidification.
image_alt: Dark mold spots spreading on a painted wall after a leak
image_caption: Warm, humid air in Hawaii lets mold grow quickly on any wet surface.
tips: Keep gutters and yard drains clear on the windward side.
Close jalousie windows tightly before heavy rain.
Use moisture absorbers or a dehumidifier in closets.
Know whether your home sits in a flood or tsunami zone.
insurance: Hurricane cover is often a separate policy or endorsement in Hawaii, so check your declarations page for wind coverage.

faq.q: Why does mold grow so fast after a leak in Hawaii?
faq.a: Mold needs moisture, warmth and food such as drywall or wood. Hawaii's warm, humid air gives it all three year-round. Start drying within 24 to 48 hours, and use dehumidifiers, not just fans.

licensing: The Hawaii Contractors License Board licenses contractors, and most repair work needs a licensed contractor and a county permit.
areas: Calls also come from Kailua-Kona, Lihue, Kapolei and Lahaina.
